Beyond the Itinerary: A Review of Faruk Moinuddin’s Sudurer Odur Duar (“Near Doors of Distant Lands”)

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-10-31

Open Faruk Moinuddin’s Sudurer Odur Duar and a question surfaces at once: is this merely a travel diary, or is the writer, under the pretext of travel, conducting a search of his own interior? Across its pages, accounts of countries near and far, inquiries into history, and the faces of ordinary people combine into an art of narration in which travel stops being mere movement and becomes a path of self-discovery. This is precisely why the book steps beyond the familiar borders of travel writing.

By travel literature we usually mean a writer’s notebook of journeys abroad, an information-rich guidebook, or a catalogue of sights to be ticked off. Moinuddin’s book is something else. It is at once a personal memoir, a search through history, a record of cultural observation, an exercise in political analysis, and, above all, a warm and humane document that keeps people at its centre. The narrative is built around the author’s journeys to Myanmar, Thailand, Hong Kong, Australia and Sri Lanka. Yet his gaze is wider than this geographical sweep. Rather than the flag, the pagoda, the gold mine or the sunlit beach, it looks for the lives of ordinary people, their sorrows and joys, their memories of history and their hopes for the future. Moinuddin travels to see places, but he returns carrying people. It is this human presence that gives his writing its life.

The title best captures what lies inside the book. Sudurer Odur Duar, “the near doorway of the far-off”: the distant countries that sit remote on the map, that guidebooks file under “places to see”, are brought by Moinuddin right up to our own threshold. Through his writing we do not merely travel; we peer into the homes of the people who live there and share in their festivals, their struggles, their griefs and dreams. Geography has its place here, but so do history, archaeology, architecture, food, dress, religion, politics, economics, and the tension between colonialism and modernity. None of these sits as an inventory entry. Each dissolves into the author’s experience and together they form a singular literary voice.

The story begins at the moment he steps into Mandalay airport. Weary from the long journey from Dhaka, the author and his companions are met by Zin, a young guide in a longyi, whose presence dispels their tiredness at first sight. Zin does more than show the way; she opens up the heart of a country. Driving from the airport into the city, they notice rows of streetlights, like those on the Dhaka–Chittagong highway. Then Zin explains that because powerful landowners blocked the authorities from acquiring the land, the road had to be built crooked. From this small detail, a deep picture of Myanmar’s land politics unfolds before the reader. In the car, Zin goes on to describe the economic reality of Myanmar: the “cronies”, who have cut deals with the government and seized control of all the major businesses, while ordinary people, preoccupied with putting rice on the table and cloth on their backs, can scarcely think about politics. Listening to her, the author realises he is facing not just a country but an entire hierarchy. Here the character of his travelling eye shows itself. He does not simply collect souvenirs; he sees the workings of power even in the bend of a road.

Watching the lit streets of Mandalay pass by, he arrives at the landing on the Irrawaddy. The name Irrawaddy, some say, derives from the Indian river Ravi; others trace it to Airavata, the elephant who carries the Hindu god Indra. Myanmar’s military rulers have changed the name to “Ayeyarwady”, but the author continues to call it Irabati. The drift of this name is a small mirror of Myanmar’s history: colonialism, empire and military rule all lie folded within it. Not far from the river landing, the high walls of the Royal Palace come into view. The history of the palace of King Mindon and his successor King Thibaw is soaked in blood. Thibaw was finally defeated by the British and exiled to Ratnagiri in India. The British seized the palace, the Japanese bombing of the Second World War nearly destroyed it, and it was restored in 1990. The author listens to this history and sees the palace’s modern incarnation, yet he does not grieve much, for he understands that a modern reconstruction of antiquity can never bring back the original. Here one side of his historical sense becomes clear: he knows that a place is not mere geography but an archaeological excavation of layers of time.One of Mandalay’s great attractions is the Sun U Ponya Shin Pagoda on Sagaing Hill. Before entering, he notices the donation boxes: a huge frog statue with a slot for coins in its belly, glass boxes with mountains of banknotes inside. On each box is written what its money will be spent on: electricity, repairs, monks’ robes, offerings. The author is impressed by how neatly devotees’ gifts are apportioned to specific purposes. Local worshippers sit praying before the Buddha image. He observes the deep self-surrender in the eyes of the nuns, and how, through their fasting and prayer, the philosophy of life of an entire community comes to the surface. He remains no mere describer of sights; he becomes an attentive reader of a culture.

Another important site in Mandalay is a Buddhist nunnery. The author arrives at high noon. The courtyard is deserted and the wide tiled steps lie empty. Adolescent girls study here the principles and practices of Buddhism. A shaven-headed girl in a pink robe is arranging bowls, spoons and cups in the shade of a distant tree. As he leaves, two girls strike a large gong beside the steps with a wooden mallet, and the sound spreads through the sleepless noon heat. Within this small scene, a Buddhist culture shows its shadow well beyond the confines of the nunnery. The author sees how a religious institution forms a stratum of society and how women find their place within this religious structure. This image will return later, before the wishing tree of Hong Kong, offering a chance to understand the relationship between faith and ritual in two different cultures.

The Hong Kong chapter opens with a train journey. From Kowloon he takes the MTR, changing trains three times, and gets off at Tai Po, from where bus 64P carries him to see the Lam Tsuen wishing tree. The tree is a Chinese banyan, and local belief holds that wishes made before it come true. The method: tie a piece of paper to an orange and throw it into the branches. If it lodges, the wish will be granted; if it falls, something overly ambitious has been asked. The author talks with an old Chinese man sitting beside the tree, and by combining his broken English with the guidebook, he learns that a camphor tree once stood here. A man, disheartened by his son’s slow progress at school, poured out his heart’s fervent desire to the tree, and from then on the boy’s studies improved. News spread, and people came to make their vows. Later the camphor tree burned down, and this banyan was planted in its place. Watching the scene, the author is amused to find the Chinese just as devoted as Indians and Bangladeshis to charms, incantations, feng shui, all of it; not even the Communist revolution could shake people’s belief. For him this observation is a significant cultural lesson: however much modernity and revolution may come, the roots of people’s elemental faith and custom run deep.

Hong Kong’s rural village of Kang Hing Wai was settled by people who fled China after the revolution of 1949. Suddenly, on the village road, a colourful procession appears: the Tin Hau festival, in honour of the sea goddess. The locals pray at this festival for safe lives, good weather and abundant fish. Here the author meets Yuki, a local girl, who shows him around the village and takes him to watch the procession. On the way Yuki says that although Hong Kongers are, as a people, anti-British, they have always felt a distance from mainland Chinese over their English education and manners. The British saw themselves as a high-caste aristocracy, while to their eyes Hong Kongers were “dirty Chinese”. Walking with Yuki, the author learns much of Hong Kong’s social history: rickshaw stands, swarms of beggars, the slums of the poor. Yuki says, “Our Eastern countries were really like this; the British changed a great deal. And Hong Kong is the showcase of capitalist economy.” For the author, Yuki’s observation becomes a vital illustration of the relationship between colonialism and capitalism.

In the Ballarat chapter in Australia, the author enters Sovereign Hill, where the appearance of the town of the 1850s has been preserved. Shops, offices, the post office, the inn, the blacksmith’s, the theatre, the bank, the church: everything belongs to that era. The people moving through the streets wear the clothes of the time: women in enormous skirts and corsets, hair pinned up, men in frock coats, ties, top hats and black gloves. Here he meets a police officer who addresses him as “sir”; surprised at first, he later understands that the people here are playing roles, as part of Sovereign Hill. The experience carries him back a hundred and fifty years to a provincial town. Yet inside this museumised town he finds the history of the gold mines, the struggles of the workers, the story of the Eureka Rebellion, which makes the place not merely a tourist attraction but a living schoolroom of the history of democracy.

The history of the Ballarat gold rush captivates him. In 1851 Edward Hargraves first discovered gold, and as the news spread, the rush began. The author descends into a mine, where the darkness of the tunnels, the steep slopes and the stone pillars carry him into another world. The most important historical event in Ballarat is the Eureka Rebellion of 1854. The miners rose against government taxes on gold mining and the licence fees. The author watches a multimedia show in which the rebellion comes alive. He sees how the miners made the Eureka flag, how they built a stockade under Peter Lalor, and how twenty-two miners were killed in the assault by police and soldiers. He learns the outcome: the government conceded many of the miners’ demands, licence fees were reduced, and voting rights were granted. The rebellion is regarded as a foundation of Australian democracy. As he leaves Sovereign Hill, the author feels how the history of one small town has shaped the democratic spirit of an entire nation. Here history does not remain merely a matter of past events; it explains the political consciousness of the present from within.

The Sri Lanka chapter begins at Colombo airport, from which he is taken to Galle, a historic town on the island’s southern coast. The Portuguese built a fort here in 1608, the Dutch seized it in 1640, and the British in 1796. The author sees the ancient fort walls and the blend of Portuguese and Dutch architecture, and the church, the lighthouse and the old buildings within the fort all seem witnesses to history. These layers of colonial architecture remind him of the long history of the European powers’ arrival in Asia.The most memorable experience of his Sri Lankan journey is whale watching off Mirissa. They reach Mirissa harbour at six in the morning. The local guide, Roy, makes them wear life jackets, by force if need be; even a Chinese tourist is obliged to comply. The author wonders aloud, “Will a culture of obeying rules ever take hold in our country?” Out at sea, as their boat rides up and down the crests of the waves, many passengers fall seasick. The author is surprised that he himself feels none, and he recalls Sarat Chandra’s novel Srikanta, where the narrator says that whatever is called seasickness had, he supposed, been used up on boats in his childhood. This memory ties his personal experience to the literary tradition. The whale-watching expedition succeeds: for a few seconds the black back of a whale is visible, then it dives. But six hours of travel and the misery of seasickness, at a price of twenty dollars: the author throws this question to the reader, laying bare the tension between the worth of the tourism industry and the physical limits of human beings.

On the return from Mirissa the author sees the local fishermen’s “ritipata”, fishing while perched on poles planted in the sea near the shore. The method was devised during the Second World War, in a time of food scarcity, and poor fishermen still practise it. He takes photographs and talks with the fishermen. He learns that the method now exists mostly for tourists, and that the fishermen take money in exchange for photographs. The author is struck by the fact that after the 2004 tsunami the marine resources of the region have dwindled greatly, and the fishermen now depend on tourists. Here the dual face of the tourist industry comes into view: on one hand it is a source of livelihood, on the other it turns heritage into commerce.

At Bentota stands the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage, said to be the largest of its kind in the world. The author comes to watch the elephants’ milk feeding. Mahouts bring milk in one-litre bottles from buckets loaded onto a trolley, and he watches two white-skinned young women hand-feed a baby elephant, while another calf stands beside it, watching with wide eyes. Here the author recalls Syed Mujtaba Ali’s story “Hati” (“The Elephant”), in which the French, Germans, Russians and Americans each offered their theories about elephants, and in the end the Indian was dismissed as biased. Through this story the author shows how ignorant Europeans are about elephants, and how hollow the claims of Western scientific superiority are. At the orphanage he sees how the elephants are raised in a natural setting: milk each day, bathing and water play at fixed times. But he realises that their lives are bound by a discipline as strict as a cadet college’s, without the freedom of the jungle. Even so, the orphanage has kept thousands of orphaned calves alive. This tension, between conservation and freedom, between human control and natural life, raises a larger question for the author.

The greatest strength of the book is its human-centred vision. In Myanmar, he gives more weight to the words of Zin, Min Min and local people than to the pagodas and monasteries. In Hong Kong, his conversation with Yuki, who explains the city’s social history, matters more to him than the wishing tree. In Sri Lanka, what lingers in memory is less the whale watching than the fishermen’s ritipata and the elephant orphanage. This habit of putting people first moves the book out of the place of the ordinary travel guide. Zin is not merely a guide; she is an interpreter of the Myanmar state. Min Min does not merely recount the history of the pagodas; he also tells the sad story of Bagan’s decline. Yuki does not merely show Hong Kong around; she reflects on the long shadow of colonialism. The fishermen do not merely pose for photographs; they lay bare the contradictions of a tourism-dependent livelihood.

Another lovely aspect of the book is that, even while looking at foreign lands, the author keeps remembering his own. The roads of Myanmar remind him of Dhaka, the U Bein Bridge of the haors of Sunamganj, the pagodas of Bagan of the great monastery at Paharpur in Bangladesh. These memories enrich his experience. Yet he never makes direct comparisons; there is no sentence like “We have nothing like this in our country.” Instead he lets memories return naturally, as though the foreign scene were unfolding some old map inside him. This makes the book more personal. Readers, too, find their own memories answering the author’s, and the foreign scenes become near to them as well.

Moinuddin’s language is simple, clear and fluent. He does not burden the reader with difficult words, yet in places deep observation and subtle humour come through. Describing a pub in Mandalay, he writes: “Since an unexpected afternoon break had come our way, the girl, with no objection to this unplanned pub visit, took us to ‘Café Jazz’. One could tell at a glance that it was meant for Mandalay’s upper-class crowd.” In this sentence he conveys not only the class character of the pub but also hints at his own powers of observation. His humour deserves particular notice. Whether it is the description of Siddhartha Huq at Yangon University as “an eye-hospital patient in a longyi,” or the haggling with the ticket-counter cashier over seeing the Buddha image at a pagoda, such scenes carry both comedy and social observation. The humour sometimes turns to self-mockery: when he jokes about his smoking habit or his ignorance of languages, the author presents himself as an ordinary person rather than a tourist, which makes his relationship with the reader more intimate.

Another strength of the book is its historical consciousness. When the author looks at the pagodas of Bagan, he sees not only architecture; he knows the history of King Anawrahta, the madness of King Narathihapate, the Mongol invasion, colonial rule, all of it. He does not give history as bare fact; he weaves it into the narrative so that the reader can see the shadow of time falling across a place. The descriptions of Myanmar’s 8888 uprising, General Ne Win’s eccentric rule and Aung San Suu Kyi’s house in particular have real historical depth and political awareness. In Australia, by narrating the Eureka Rebellion, he shows how a small rebellion can become the foundation of a democracy. These historical layers make the book more than a travelogue; it takes on the character of a cultural and political reading as well.

The book does have some limitations. In places the abundance of information slows the pace of the narrative, particularly in the history of Bagan and the statistics of the gold rush. Had these been condensed, the book would have moved more briskly. This surfeit of detail occasionally overwhelms the reader, especially when long lists of kings, wars, dates and figures arrive. Elsewhere, the travelling companions remain secondary; their reactions and feelings stay centred on the author. Rupali, Siddhartha Huq and Tushar Das often stay in the background, and their own thoughts are not brought forward. Another limitation is that the voices of local people are sometimes not heard directly; we know them through the author, not through their own telling. Had there been more dialogue or interviews, the book’s human-centred vision would have been stronger still.

The title Sudurer Odur Duar expresses the book’s true meaning. Moinuddin has travelled to distant countries, Myanmar, Thailand, Hong Kong, Australia and Sri Lanka, but he has brought those faraway countries right to our doorstep. Through his writing we walk the roads of Myanmar with Zin, climb the pagodas of Bagan with Min Min, stand before Hong Kong’s wishing tree with Yuki, read the history of the Eureka Rebellion alongside Peter Lalor, and watch the Sri Lankan fishermen perch on their ritipata poles. This book is not just a travel guide; it weaves together human faces, the memory of history, clashes of culture and the influence of modernity. The author shows how the roads, food, dress, religion and politics of a country combine to form a living text. And in making this text, he has repeatedly tested his own eyes and questioned his own preconceptions.

In the tradition of Bengali travel writing, this book is a notable addition. Bangladeshi writers have generally looked at and written about Western countries, but Moinuddin has drawn a different map, centred on Asia’s neighbouring countries. His gaze is not only that of a tourist but also that of a historian and a social scientist. He sees how power, class, colonialism and modernity shape human lives. Through this book he proves that good travel writing depends not only on what is seen but on how it is seen. To travel is not merely to go to a distant country; it is to make that country one’s own, to learn to know its people, to feel their lives. In every chapter of his book Faruk Moinuddin does exactly this, opening the door of the far-off and showing us the people who live near. That is why the book does not stay merely travel literature; it becomes literature. After finishing it, the reader will remember not just some facts about a few countries or a map of sights, but will be compelled to reflect on the deep bond between place and people, the cruelty of history, and the complex layers of culture.
